8 questions. Click an answer to check it: you will see right away whether it is correct, with a short explanation. Nothing is saved.

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**1.** What makes a problem "unsupervised"?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- The model is trained without a test set
- There is no target variable: we only have the features X
- Nobody checks the results
- The data has missing values
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
In supervised learning, each observation comes with a target Y that the model learns to predict. In unsupervised learning, there is no Y: we look for a structure inside X, for example groups of similar observations.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="2"}
**2.** What are the two steps repeated by the K-Means algorithm?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Split the worst cluster in two, then merge the two closest clusters
- Draw new random centres, then keep the best ones
- Assign each point to its nearest centre, then move each centre to the mean of its points
- Remove the outliers, then compute the mean of the data
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
Step 1 (assignment) and step 2 (update) both lower the inertia. The loop stops when no point changes cluster.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="3"}
**3.** The inertia of a K-Means clustering is...

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- The number of iterations needed to converge
- The mean distance between the centres
- The silhouette score multiplied by K
- The sum of the squared distances between each point and the centre of its cluster
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
K-Means looks for the clusters with the smallest inertia (within-cluster sum of squares). It always decreases when K grows, so it cannot be used alone to choose K: look for the elbow of the curve.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**4.** Two runs of K-Means on the same data give different clusters. Why?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- K-Means has a bug
- The result depends on the initial centres: a run can stop in a local minimum
- The data changes between two runs
- K-Means is a supervised method
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
K-Means only guarantees a local minimum of the inertia. The k-means++ start spreads the initial centres, and `n_init=10` runs the algorithm 10 times and keeps the run with the lowest inertia.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="2"}
**5.** Why should you standardise the variables before K-Means?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Because K-Means only accepts values between 0 and 1
- To make the algorithm converge faster
- Because K-Means uses distances: a variable with large values (an income in euros) would dominate a variable with small values (an age)
- It is not needed for K-Means
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
The Euclidean distance adds up the gaps of all the variables. Without scaling, the clusters only follow the variables measured in large numbers. `StandardScaler` gives every variable the same weight.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="2"}
**6.** A point has a silhouette of -0.2. What does it mean?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- It is perfectly placed in its cluster
- It is an outlier that K-Means removed
- It is closer, on average, to the nearest other cluster than to its own: it is probably in the wrong cluster
- The silhouette cannot be negative
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
$s(i)=\frac{b(i)-a(i)}{\max(a(i),b(i))}$, where $a(i)$ is the mean distance to its own cluster and $b(i)$ the mean distance to the nearest other cluster. It is negative when $a(i) > b(i)$.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="3"}
**7.** The elbow method suggests K = 3 and the silhouette score is highest for K = 2. What should you do?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Always follow the silhouette score
- Take K = 2.5
- Always follow the elbow method
- Look at both clusterings, interpret them, and decide with your knowledge of the field
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
These methods are guides, not judges. On the Iris flowers, K = 2 isolates one very clear species, and K = 3 also separates two species that look alike. Both are true; the use of the clusters decides.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-q data-answer="1"}
**8.** On which data does K-Means struggle, even with a perfect initialisation?

::: {.sb-quiz-options}
- Round clusters of similar size, well separated
- Clusters with non-convex shapes (like half-moons) or with very different sizes and densities
- Data with more than 100 observations
- Data with two variables
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-explain}
Each point goes to its nearest centre, so the border between two clusters is a straight line halfway between the centres. K-Means builds round, convex clusters of similar width. DBSCAN, in the next section, handles other shapes.
:::
:::

::: {.sb-quiz-score}
